titre: Vitruvius’s triad owes its famous form to Wotton, in 1624
accroche: Vitruvius writes “solidity, utility, beauty” within a classification. In 1624, Wotton draws the English motto from it and judges the division misplaced in Vitruvius.
contenu_vulgarise:
Vitruvius, a Roman author of the 1st century BCE, is famous for three qualities every building should combine: solidity, utility, beauty, sometimes called the Vitruvian virtues. The passage, however, is narrower than the formula, and the most quoted motto, in English “commodity, firmness and delight,” is not his.

## What Vitruvius writes

The treatise De architectura, probably written between 30 and 20 BCE and dedicated to the emperor Augustus, devotes its first book to the foundations of the art. Chapter 2 defines architecture through six notions: ordinatio, dispositio, eurythmia, symmetria, decor, and distributio. Chapter 3 moves on to another subject: it divides architecture into three parts, construction, gnomonics (sundials), and mechanics. Construction is in turn divided in two: city walls and public works on the one hand, private buildings on the other. Public works are of three kinds: defense (walls, towers, gates), religion (temples), and common use (harbors, forums, porticoes, baths, theaters, promenades).

Then comes the famous sentence, in paragraph 2: “Haec autem ita fieri debent, ut habeatur ratio firmitatis, utilitatis, venustatis.” That is, in substance: this must be done with regard to solidity, utility, beauty (the card’s own translation). Vitruvius spells out each term. Solidity comes from foundations sunk down to firm ground and a choice of materials made without miserliness. Utility comes from an arrangement of spaces that does not hinder use. Beauty comes from a pleasing and elegant appearance, with correct proportions among the parts.

The word “Haec,” “this,” follows directly on the list of city walls, temples, and public places. The text does not say at this point whether the sentence also extends to private buildings, which the chapter has just mentioned: that is a question of interpretation. What is certain is that the triad does not open the treatise as a definition of architecture. It concludes a classification, whereas the chapter that defines architecture has six notions.

## What Wotton makes of it

In 1624, the Englishman Henry Wotton publishes The Elements of Architecture in London, presenting it as a compilation drawn from the best authors and the best examples. He begins by stating that the art of building has an end, to build well, and then writes: “Well building hath three Conditions. Commodity, firmness, and Delight.” He adds that this is a common division among authors in the field, but that Vitruvius himself has, he says without knowing how, somewhat misplaced it, in Book I, chapter 3. Wotton thus does not present it as the founding principle of Vitruvius’s treatise: he speaks of a common division whose placement in the ancient text he finds questionable.

The order differs too. In Vitruvius, solidity comes first. Wotton puts commodity first. According to Wikipedia, which relies on a scholarly work, this order was changed as early as the 15th century by Leon Battista Alberti, then taken up in the 16th by Palladio, apparently Wotton’s source. The motto, incidentally, circulates today in both orders: the Wikipedia article devoted to it is titled “Firmness, commodity, and delight.”

## What this changes

Vitruvius is quoted in three words as if he had founded the discipline on them. The Latin text shows a sentence placed in a classification chapter, and a motto that owes its form to Renaissance readers and to an English author of the 17th century. The preceding chapter has six notions that gave rise to no comparable motto. Why did the three words become a motto, and not the six?

carte.punch: “Commodity, firmness and delight” is Wotton, 1624: Vitruvius writes these three words differently.
carte.idee: In Vitruvius, solidity, utility, and beauty conclude a classification of public works, in Book I, chapter 3, with solidity first. The English motto “commodity, firmness and delight,” with commodity first, is Henry Wotton’s, in 1624. He judges the division misplaced in Vitruvius.

The transcription of Wotton’s book, whose first page sets out the division into commodity, firmness, and delight.

quiz.question: In De architectura, where is the sentence on solidity, utility, and beauty found?
choix: At the opening of the treatise, as a definition of architecture
In the chapter that defines architecture through six notions
In the chapter on Greek temples and the orders
In the classification chapter, after the list of public works
quiz.explication: The sentence comes in Book I, chapter 3, right after the city walls, temples, and public places. Chapter 2 is the one with the six notions. It is neither the opening of the treatise nor a passage on the orders.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who gave the triad its English form “commodity, firmness and delight”?
choix: Henry Wotton, in The Elements of Architecture, in 1624
Vitruvius himself, in Latin, with the words “commodity, firmness, delight”
Palladio, in I quattro libri dell'architettura
John Ruskin, in The Seven Lamps of Architecture
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The English formula comes from Wotton, in 1624. Vitruvius’s Latin says firmitas, utilitas, venustas. Palladio writes in Italian, and Ruskin, in the 19th century, adds other notions such as sacrifice and obedience.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Wotton say about the division into three conditions in relation to Vitruvius?
choix: That it is Vitruvius’s original discovery, not to be altered
That it is common among authors, but somewhat misplaced in Vitruvius himself
That it is Wotton’s own invention, unknown to Vitruvius
That it is borrowed from Cicero, from whom Vitruvius would have taken it
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Wotton writes that it is a common division among authors, somewhat misplaced by Vitruvius himself in Book I, chapter 3. He presents it neither as his own invention nor as the founding principle of the treatise.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the order of the three qualities in Vitruvius, and in Wotton?
choix: Utility, solidity, beauty in Vitruvius; solidity, utility, beauty in Wotton
Solidity, utility, beauty in Vitruvius; commodity, firmness, delight in Wotton
Solidity, beauty, utility in Vitruvius; utility, beauty, solidity in Wotton
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Vitruvius writes firmitas, utilitas, venustas. Wotton writes “Commodity, firmness, and Delight”: commodity moves to the front.
